results.title: Medium
results.content:
1. \\Short contexts (<4K tokens):\\ The compression overhead exceeds the memory savings. Below 4K, the KV cache is small enough that FP16 is fine.

2. \\Latency-critical single-request serving:\\ TurboQuant adds ~15ms of compression/decompression overhead per forward pass. For single-user chat where p99 matters more than throughput, this can hurt.

3. \\Models with <13B parameters:\\ Smaller models have proportionally smaller KV caches. The memory savings don’t justify the compute overhead. [...] The KV cache was the last major memory bottleneck in LLM serving. TurboQuant eliminates it. The question isn’t whether to adopt it — it’s how fast your infrastructure team can deploy it.

\\Key Takeaways:\\

- TurboQuant compresses KV cache 6x (3-bit keys, 2-bit values) with <1% quality loss

- Real benchmark: 8x batch throughput on H100 GPUs, $267K annual savings per cluster

- Deploy today via community Triton kernels + vLLM integration [...] The KV cache is the single biggest memory bottleneck in LLM inference. For a 70B model serving 128K context, the KV cache alone eats 40GB+ of GPU VRAM. That’s more memory than the model weights on most setups.

Google just solved this. Their TurboQuant algorithm, presented at ICLR 2026, compresses the KV cache to 3 bits per element — a 6x reduction — with zero measurable accuracy degradation. No retraining. No fine-tuning. No calibration data. It operates purely at inference time.

results.title: What Is Google TurboQuant? The KV Cache Compression That ...
results.content:
Before TurboQuant, most production systems stored KV cache in 16-bit (FP16 or BF16). Some aggressive deployments used 8-bit (INT8). Getting to 3 bits with no meaningful accuracy loss is a significant jump.

To put it concretely:

   A KV cache that previously required 60GB of GPU memory could be compressed to roughly 11GB.
   A single H100 with 80GB HBM could serve contexts or batch sizes that previously required multiple GPUs.
   Serving costs per token drop substantially. [...] Weight quantization (methods like GPTQ, AWQ, and GGUF formats used in llama.cpp) compresses the model’s learned parameters. This reduces the memory needed to load the model, but it doesn’t directly address runtime KV cache growth.

KV cache quantization — what TurboQuant does — targets the activations stored during inference. These grow dynamically with context length and batch size. They’re the problem that explodes in production. [...] For inference at scale, the KV cache often consumes more memory than the model weights themselves. A 70B parameter model might need around 140GB for weights — but serving it with long contexts across large batches can demand hundreds of gigabytes more for KV storage.

results.title: TurboQuant: the new(?) and controversial ground breaking ...
results.content: TurboQuant is Google’s proposed approach to one of the most consequential unsolved problems in production large language model efficiency: what do you do when the memory your model needs during inference grows faster than your hardware budget? KV cache compression is where that question gets answered or doesn’t, and TurboQuant claims to have cracked it. We’ll look at the benchmarks, surface an active academic controversy that most mainstream coverage has ignored entirely, and pull in what real [...] The key-value (KV) cache is the memory structure that allows transformer models to “remember” everything they’ve seen in a conversation or document during inference. Without it, the model would have to reprocess the entire context from scratch on every token generation step. The problem is architectural and unforgiving: KV cache memory grows linearly with both sequence length and batch size, which means serving real users at scale pushes it past comfortable limits fast. [...] To make this concrete, consider a 70B parameter model serving 100 concurrent requests at a 32,000-token context window. At standard BF16 precision, the KV cache alone can consume well over 100GB of GPU memory, potentially more than the model weights themselves. That’s not a theoretical edge case; that’s a Tuesday afternoon for anyone running a serious inference cluster.

results.title: KV Cache Is Eating Your VRAM. Here's How Google Fixed ...
results.content: Though KV cache came as a silver lining for LLMs, it brought up more challenges. It introduced additional memory overhead. This might not be a big issue for SLMs, but mega-LLMs with billions of parameters now became more difficult to load on machines. Roughly 20-30% additional VRAM is consumed by the KV cache alone.
